text: Staging is a safe place to fail — this lesson is about using that safety on purpose, by actually checking staged data before it moves any further.

Four checks belong in nearly every staging process. Null checks, for columns the business genuinely requires a value in. Referential integrity checks, confirming a fact row's dimension key actually exists before it loads. Duplicate checks, catching the same source row landing twice. And type or format checks, catching a malformed value staging's loose typing let through on purpose, before it has to become a strict warehouse column.

Finding a bad row is only half the job. Reject and log it to a quarantine table when the business can't safely guess a value. Default and flag it — substituting a known placeholder — when a missing value shouldn't block the whole row. Or fail the entire batch when loading any of it would be worse than loading none of it. Whichever you pick, never just quietly drop the row with no record it happened.
Data that clears every one of these checks is finally trustworthy — but you still need to know exactly where it came from and when it arrived. That's next lesson: auditing and lineage columns.
